Right: the new graph keeps just those four nodes and the three edges among them, A–B, B–C, and B–E; nodes D and F and every edge touching them are dropped, shown dashed." width="100%"} Extracts the currently selected nodes or edges into a new Graph object. The behavior depends on what's selected: - nodes selected: include those nodes plus all edges between them - edges selected: include those edges plus their endpoint nodes Nodes and edges keep their IDs, labels, weights and attributes, so results can be matched back to the original graph by ID. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : New Graph object containing the subgraph, with the same directedness and weighting as the original graph. Empty if nothing is selected. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~select_nodes`) : Select the nodes that pass a test. [](`~select_edges`) : Select the edges that pass a test. [](`~subgraph`) : Extract the induced subgraph on a set of nodes. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The selected nodes and the edges among them become a new graph. `ec.friends()` is a network of friendships among the members of a chess club and a climbing club, and the 12 climbers have 18 friendships among them: ::: {#b3067ad1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec friends = ec.friends() friends.select_nodes(lambda n: n.attributes["club"] == "Climbing") climbing = friends.transform_to_subgraph_ws() climbing.count_nodes(), climbing.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (12, 18) ``` ::: ::: With an edge selection, the selected edges and their endpoints are kept instead. The 10 friendships made since 2022 involve 17 people: ::: {#08551dd2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} friends.select_edges(lambda e: e.attributes["since"] >= 2022) recent = friends.transform_to_subgraph_ws() recent.count_nodes(), recent.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (17, 10) ``` ::: :::
